title: Voltage-Dependent, Compartment-Specific Plasticity

html:
Perhaps the most useful way to write cortex-specific plasticity laws is in a voltage-first form: local synaptic change is driven by presynaptic input timing interacting with the postsynaptic dendritic voltage trajectory at or near the synapse. Under this framing, apparently distinct empirical traditions–pair-based STDP, rate-dependent plasticity, and dendrite-centered plasticity–are not separate rule families so much as different operating regimes of the same underlying state variable, namely local membrane potential Vm(t)V_m(t). What matters for a synapse is not whether the neuron emitted a spike in some abstract sense, but what voltage waveform the synapse actually experienced, on both fast and slower timescales, as presynaptic input arrived. A 2025 in-vivo study finds different plasticity predictors in apical and basal dendrites (Figure). Dendritic location changes how voltage shapes plasticity (Figure).

A canonical realization of this idea in cortex is the family of voltage-dependent STDP rules associated with Clopath and related models 1, 2. In these models, synaptic updates depend jointly on presynaptic spike arrival and postsynaptic membrane potential, typically through a combination of an instantaneous voltage term and one or more low-pass filtered voltage traces, often alongside a presynaptic eligibility trace. Pair-based STDP then appears not as the fundamental rule, but as a special case that emerges under particular voltage trajectories induced by pre/post spike pairing. This reframing is important because it replaces a spike-centric description with a biophysically closer one: the effective control variable for plasticity is the local postsynaptic state, not the symbolic occurrence of a pre-post spike pair.

Mechanistically, the rule says that potentiation requires a sufficiently strong and fast depolarizing event–for example, coincidence between an EPSP and a backpropagating action potential, or between clustered synaptic input and a local dendritic spike–embedded within a permissive longer-timescale depolarization context captured by a filtered voltage trace 1. Depression, by contrast, is favored when presynaptic activation occurs in more moderate depolarization regimes that are insufficient to cross the potentiation boundary but still drive a plasticity-relevant postsynaptic state. In this way, a single voltage-based formulation reproduces many of the nonlinearities that historically made the plasticity literature look fragmented: timing-window asymmetries, frequency dependence, voltage-clamp dependence, and the classical LTP/LTD induction protocols can all be understood without treating somatic spikes themselves as the primitive variable 1.

This is why voltage, rather than spikes, is the right control variable. The proximate gate on synaptic change is the voltage experienced locally at the synapse and in its parent dendritic compartment. Somatic action potentials and their backpropagation are only one source of such depolarization. Others include summed EPSPs, NMDA spikes, dendritic Ca2+^{2+} spikes, and plateau-like regenerative events, all of which can provide the local depolarization needed to trigger plasticity even when the soma does not emit a conventional output spike 1. A voltage-based rule therefore generalizes naturally beyond simple spike pairing and is better matched to the compartmental structure of pyramidal neurons, where different dendritic domains can experience qualitatively different voltage landscapes during the same behavioral event.

Once the rule is local in this sense, dendritic location dependence falls out almost automatically. The same phenomenological plasticity rule can yield different outcomes at proximal versus distal synapses because the voltage waveform differs with dendritic location: backpropagating action potentials attenuate with distance from the soma, branch-specific nonlinearities such as NMDA or Ca2+^{2+} spikes are easier to trigger in some compartments than others, and ion-channel densities vary systematically across the arbor. Modeling work shows that many seemingly paradoxical findings–including LTP without somatic spikes, frequency-dependent inversions of timing rules, and apparent reversals of the sign of plasticity with dendritic location–can be explained as lawful consequences of differences in local Vm(t)V_m(t) rather than as evidence for fundamentally different plasticity mechanisms 3. A complementary, more explicitly dendrite-centric framework extends this logic further by introducing multiple post- and presynaptic pathways in a biophysically realistic pyramidal neuron and showing that a range of landmark “contradictory” protocols can be reconciled once dendritic propagation and synapse location are modeled directly 4. From this perspective, calcium-threshold models are best understood as a downstream biophysical implementation of the same principle. Local voltage dynamics determine NMDA conductance, activation of voltage-gated calcium channels, regenerative dendritic events, and calcium release from intracellular stores; the resulting Ca2+^{2+} transient then determines whether the synapse crosses an LTD-like or LTP-like induction threshold 5. Voltage-based rules thus provide the phenomenology, while calcium-threshold rules provide the more explicit biophysical substrate. The two are not competing accounts so much as different descriptive levels of the same update machinery. In the same spirit, normative dendritic-prediction schemes in which apical-basal mismatch encodes an error signal can be read as specifying which voltage configuration should occur if learning is to happen, while voltage-dependent plasticity rules specify how that configuration is converted into synaptic change.

Recent in vivo work strongly supports the idea that a unified voltage/calcium-dependent plasticity machinery can nevertheless produce compartment-specific effective rules within a single cortical pyramidal neuron 6. In mouse motor cortex during naturalistic learning, Wright et al. found that potentiation in apical dendrites is best predicted by local coactivity among nearby spines: plasticity events tend to cluster spatially along apical branches, consistent with a cooperative, branch-local rule. In basal dendrites, by contrast, potentiation is better predicted by synaptic activity coincident with postsynaptic output, i.e, a more classical output-referenced Hebbian rule. This dissociation is especially telling because it occurs within the same neuron. It implies that cortical pyramidal cells do not implement a single homogeneous learning rule across their arbor; instead, the effective rule depends on the dendritic compartment in which the synapse is embedded and on the voltage/calcium regime that compartment typically inhabits during behavior. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

The causal asymmetry is equally informative. When postsynaptic spiking is blocked, basal potentiation is selectively disrupted, whereas apical plasticity is much less affected 6. Apical plasticity is therefore not simply “ordinary STDP with a weaker backpropagating spike.” It is mechanistically distinct and can be largely output-independent, relying instead on branch-local cooperativity and dendritic nonlinearities. In computational terms, basal synapses appear to learn mainly from features that successfully contributed to the neuron’s emitted code, whereas apical synapses appear to learn from the co-occurrence structure of contextual or feedback inputs at the branch level. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

A direct biophysical mechanism for this apical cooperativity is provided by calcium-based heterosynaptic interaction among neighboring spines 7. Bhatt et al. show that calcium influx at an active spine can diffuse to nearby unstimulated spines, with the sign and magnitude of the induced heterosynaptic plasticity depending on inter-spine distance, timing, spine-neck geometry, buffering, and store-mediated amplification. This provides a concrete mechanism for the clustered apical rule seen in vivo: an active spine can generate a local calcium plume that effectively tags neighboring spines on the same branch for potentiation or depression, even if those neighbors were not driven by precisely coincident presynaptic spikes. In distal apical compartments, where somatic backpropagation is attenuated and plasticity depends more heavily on local NMDA- and Ca2+^{2+}-dependent dendritic events, this kind of diffusion-mediated coupling creates a genuine branch-level credit-assignment mechanism. Inputs that are nearby on the dendrite and roughly co-timed become bound into a functional cluster, regardless of whether the cell fired an output spike.

The computational interpretation is therefore a clean one. Basal plasticity approximates credit assignment to the neuron’s emitted code: synapses are strengthened when they help drive the output that the neuron actually produced. Apical plasticity, by contrast, approximates credit assignment to a branch-local latent cause or context model: co-active inputs are bound together into dendritic subunits that can later act as nonlinear contextual features or top-down hypotheses 6, 7. The important point is that these are not two unrelated learning systems. They are two emergent operating regimes of a common voltage/calcium-dependent plasticity machinery, expressed through different compartmental biophysics.

Overall, these results resolve much of the long-standing apparent conflict between “Hebbian,” “non-Hebbian,” “spike-based,” and “dendritic” accounts of cortical plasticity. Cortex does not need a proliferation of qualitatively unrelated rules to explain its phenomenology. A single local voltage- and calcium-dependent update framework, when embedded in the real geometry of pyramidal dendrites and the compartment-specific propagation of signals through that geometry, is sufficient to produce very different effective plasticity laws across synapses, branches, and layers. The apparent diversity of cortical learning rules is therefore, to a substantial extent, the visible consequence of a unified underlying mechanism operating in different dendritic regimes.
